query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, exposure to high-temperature oxidation and corrosive environments promotes the diffusion-driven precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases from an initially metastable, homogeneous solid-solution state. These precipitates locally modify the oxide scale formation during high-temperature exposure and create galvanic sites that accelerate corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A metastable, supersaturated solid-solution state with Mg uniformly distributed within the lightweight high-entropy alloy matrix.
generation.intervention: Controlled aging or heat treatment in an environment that promotes oxidation and corrosion, such as exposure to high-temperature air or an accelerated corrosive NaCl solution.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted at elevated temperatures (around 700°C) in air for oxidation, and under standardized immersion in NaCl solution for corrosion tests, with comparisons made against as-cast or rapidly quenched baseline samples that preserve the non-equilibrium state.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates within the alloy matrix.
generation.mechanism: During thermal exposure, Mg atoms diffuse and nucleate as a separate intermetallic phase. This phase separation undermines the uniform protective oxide layer by introducing compositional heterogeneity and localized electrochemical differences, resulting in enhanced oxidation protection under high temperature (through modified oxide scale adherence/composition) and increased corrosion rates via galvanic coupling in a corrosive environment.
generation.predicted_outcome: Aged samples will exhibit distinct microstructural demarcation with Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates, together with a modified oxide scale (potentially more adherent or compositionally distinct) at high temperature and an accelerated corrosion rate due to galvanic effects compared to the baseline material.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or rapidly quenched alloy retaining a homogeneous metastable solid-solution without significant intermetallic precipitation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for lightweight high-entropy alloys with densities below 6 g/cm³ and compositions that include sufficient Mg to drive phase separation under the tested thermal and corrosive conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of Mg diffusion, the detailed morphology of the precipitates, and their precise quantitative impact on corrosion and oxidation behavior remain to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set is rapidly quenched (baseline) and the other is subjected to an aging heat treatment at 700°C in air and separately in an NaCl solution. Employ TEM and XRD to assess phase evolution and identify the formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. Conduct electrochemical tests to measure corrosion rates and perform surface analyses (e.g., XPS, SEM) to evaluate the composition and adherence of the high-temperature oxide scales.
measurements: TEM/XRD for detection and quantification of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates
Surface characterization of oxide scales (composition and adhesion tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if aging does not lead to the formation of significant Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates, or if there is no notable difference in the corrosion rates and oxide scale properties between the aged samples and the baseline.
